newsitem.title: USA: Old jalopies may be vintage cars rising in value.
newsitem.headline: Old jalopies may be vintage cars rising in value.

text.p: Want a classy, fun car but can't afford a new Ferrari whose value drops the moment you drive it out of the showroom?

Go vintage. For as little as a few thousand dollars you can pick up an eye-catching piece of art on wheels that is unlikely to lose value and may even appreciate as much as 20 percent over the next year.

"They're mainly cars of leisure, pleasure and fun. You can drive around and have great time while still making money," said Dean Kruse, chairman of Kruse International, the world's largest collector car auction firm, based in Auburn, Ind.
But for car fans, it's not the money that counts.

"Mostly collectors see the automobile as an art form that is different from other collectibles. It is three-dimensional. There's the smell, touch, the noise," said David Gooding, head of Christie's newly formed International Motor Cars Ltd. unit.

While cars that are no longer widely available are loosely called "vintage," the term, strictly speaking, refers to models at least 60 years old, said Tad Burness, a syndicated columnist for 40 years on the field. Older ones are antiques, while more recent ones are special interest cars.
"A classic is exclusive, hand-built, customised," he said.
Cars designed by Ettore Bugatti, born in Milan in 1881, top the list of the most expensive at auction.
Kruse International has sold an all-original 1933 Bugatti Kellnar Royale Coupe for $11.5 million, and a 1931 Bugatti Royale Berline DeVoyage four-door for $6.5 million.

At Christie's in 1987, a 1931 Bugatti Royale -- one of six produced for kings and heads of state -- fetched $10.6 million. In the depths of the Depression the car sold for $40,000, when a Ford Model A cost just $700, said Gooding.

Collector Ben Rose -- who keeps his vintage race cars in a climate-controlled glass and steel pavilion featured in the 1986 movie "Ferris Bueller's Day Off" -- will sell his collection through Christie's on April 26. A 1927 Type 35B Bugatti is estimated to fetch $400,000 to $600,000.

The Duesenberg Motor Co. of Auburn, Ind., which made only about 500 cars from 1921 through 1937, also dominates the multimillion dollar list. In an age when most cars had 50 to 60 horsepower, Duesenbergs had 265 horsepower and chrome exhausts coming out of oversized hoods. The company's headquarters in Auburn is now a museum.
Other top names include Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Cadillac, Stutz, Mercedes-Benz, Alfa Romeo and Packard.

Non-classic vintage cars are far more available, though, and suit just about any budget. For the investment minded, Kruse issues an annual list of 10 collectible cars he believes will soar in value over the coming year.

Topping the 1997 list are the two-seat Allard J-2 or J2X racing cars from 1950 through 1954, which "have been big in Europe for several years, but under priced in the U.S." The cars are available for $35,000 to $50,000 and could go up by 15 percent to 20 percent in a year, Kruse said.
A jeep-like Austin Mini-Moke from 1962 through 1970 costs just $3,000 to $5,000, and could soar by 20 percent in a year.
A 1950 Buick 70 Series Roadmaster Convertible, which originally cost $2,981, is now worth $19,500 to $44,000. But Kruse expects the value to go up 15 percent in 12 months.

For novices, Kruse advises buying a 17- or 18-year-old sporty convertible, such as a 1979 Ford sports car or 1977 Chevy. "The rule of thumb is 20 years is when it starts to go up in value," he said. Red and black are the safest colours in terms of resale value, he added.

"If you want a bargain, get something from 1970s," such as big Mercuries and Oldmobiles, Burness advised. "Some states are (coming) down on these cars because they consider them polluters. They don't have much market value. Now's the time to buy."

The choice depends on what the buyer wants to do with it. If you like to show off your car at special events, get one in "perfect" condition, that is, restored and rebuilt to look brand new, Kruse said. For hobbyists who enjoy fixing cars, there are bargains galore.

To shop around, get Hemming's Motor News, with about 1,000 pages of classified advertisements for old cars worldwide. It's available at book stores for $5. To compare prices, check the 1997 Collector Vehicle Auction Results and Collector Guide by Kruse International (800 968-4444).

The vintage car market is expected to get stronger as it continues to recover from a slump in 1989 and 1990, experts said. "But don't buy a good deal if you don't like it," Kruse said. "That's what this is all about. You can invest and have fun at the same time."
